text: Why did her stepfather grip Helen Stoner's wrist so hard?
why: A plain question the story has given reason to ask: the wrist bruises are shown and the stepfather's violent temper has been described at length.

text: Why did her stepfather grip Helen Stoner's wrist so hard? — an ordinary fit of temper
why: The story establishes Dr. Roylott's uncontrollable anger and violent brawls, so an ordinary fit of temper is a possibility a reader could reasonably consider.

text: Why did her stepfather grip Helen Stoner's wrist so hard? — a quarrel about the wedding or the money
id: q.why_gripped=a quarrel about the wedding or the money
why: Money and the wedding have both been discussed (the allowance, the money she paid him, his consent to the marriage), so this is a reasonable possibility to consider.

text: Why did her stepfather grip Helen Stoner's wrist so hard? — he caught her watching or questioning him
id: q.why_gripped=he caught her watching or questioning him
why: This is a generic possibility a reader could raise given the stepfather's temper and Helen's secretive early departure, though the story has not yet shown her watching or questioning him.

text: Why did her stepfather grip Helen Stoner's wrist so hard? — to keep her from leaving the house
id: q.why_gripped=to keep her from leaving the house
why: The story has shown the household is locked and controlled, and that Helen slipped away to Holmes, so keeping her from leaving is a possibility she has reason to consider.

text: Why did her stepfather grip Helen Stoner's wrist so hard? — he meant no great harm and does not know his own strength
id: q.why_gripped=he meant no great harm and does not know his own strength
why: This is Helen's own suggestion in ¶74 ('perhaps he hardly knows his own strength'), so the story has stated it.

text: Who or what is the lady in black so afraid of? — the marks of a hand are on her wrist, and she says of her stepfather that he is a hard man
why: The wrist marks are shown and Helen herself calls her stepfather 'a hard man'; her terror has been tied to the household throughout, so the observation's facts are all stated, though its wording comes close to naming the answer.
